sweep_summary: Single sweep item, Jacobsen 2000 (Phonetica 57: 40-67), is squarely about word stress in West Greenlandic and contradicts the catalog's fixed-dominant final coding: its abstract concludes 'Greenlandic prosody does not include an autonomous stress category'. Full text remains closed on every access channel checked (OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, OpenAIRE; the DOI now lands at degruyterbrill.com, Karger returns 403); only the PubMed abstract is held. Priority high for acquisition (Harvard online via HarvardKey). Re-read on-disk material corroborates: Nagano-Madsen 1993:147 (no lexical stress or accent; perceived prominence = H of the terminal contour) and Arnhold, Elfner & Compton 2023 ms pp. 5-7 (Rischel 1974:91 'no well-defined status', listeners split between antepenultimate and final vowel = the two H points of the word-final HLH contour; Jacobsen finds no autonomous stress). Recommendation unchanged from the earlier pass: recode kala1399 to no-word-stress (domain WORD) with Fortescue 1984:339 as the full-text deciding quote and Jacobsen 2000 abstract + Nagano-Madsen 1993:147 as backing; note the word-final HLH contour as the source of Gordon 2002's 'final'.

new_statements.quote: It is concluded that Greenlandic prosody does not include an autonomous stress category, either tonal or durational parameters alone will do. And although Greenlandic has distinctive quantity, there is room for considerable durational variation of segments.
new_statements.citation: Jacobsen, Birgitte. 2000. The question of 'stress' in West Greenlandic: An acoustic investigation of rhythmicization, intonation, and syllable weight. Phonetica 57(1): 40-67. doi:10.1159/000028458
new_statements.locator: Abstract, p. 40 (read via PubMed PMID 10867570; full text not obtained)
new_statements.reading: The only instrumental study devoted to West Greenlandic stress finds no autonomous word-stress category: what listeners hear as prominence is the word-final HLH pitch contour on the last vowel morae (high on the antepenultimate and final mora) plus syllable-weight duration, not stress. This flatly contradicts the catalog's fixed-dominant 'final' coding, which rests only on Gordon 2002's appendix line with no quotation. It agrees with the catalog's own domain quote (Fortescue 1984:339, 'Stress does not play any contrastive or demarcative role in West Greenlandic') and with Nagano-Madsen 1993:147 (on file, read this sweep: 'there is no lexical category of stress or accent in West Greenlandic Eskimo. The perceived prominence was found to coincide with the high tone of the terminal contour'). Caveat: abstract only; the full paper (pp. 40-67) is paywalled at De Gruyter Brill.

sources.quote: The main purpose is to investigate whether stress is a relevant category in Greenlandic word prosody. I focus on tonal and durational parameters. The data material consists of word lists read aloud seven times by two subjects. The main findings are: (1) The prosodic characteristics of words can be explained in either tonal or durational terms. [...] It is concluded that Greenlandic prosody does not include an autonomous stress category, either tonal or durational parameters alone will do.
sources.note: Dedicated acoustic study of West Greenlandic word prosody (word lists, two speakers, seven repetitions, f0 and duration). Conclusion: no autonomous stress category in Greenlandic prosody; the word-level prominence pattern is reducible to tone (the word-final HLH contour on the last vowel morae) or to duration (syllable weight: short/long/overlong). No stress-placement rule is given because stress is denied. Arnhold, Elfner & Compton 2023 (accepted ms on file, lines 300-317) summarize the full paper the same way: antepenultimate-mora syllable has consistently higher f0 but is not longer; 'Jaco…

sources.citation: Nagano-Madsen, Yasuko. 1993. Phrase-final intonation in West Greenlandic Eskimo. Working Papers (Lund University, Dept. of Linguistics) 40: 145-155.
sources.quote: p.146: 'What is now recognized as being an element of phrase-final intonation manifestation on the last three vowel morae (Rischel 1974) has earlier been interpreted as "musical accent" (Thalbitzer 1904) or "stress" (Pyle 1970). Both Rischel and Nagano-Madsen 1992 treat the language as having no lexical stress or accent and as being mora-counting.' p.148: 'there is no lexical category of stress or accent in West Greenlandic Eskimo. The perceived prominence was found to coincide with the high tone of the terminal contour, be that phrase-internal or phrase-final.'

sources.quote: p.1-2: 'Kleinschmidt ... recognized that stress placement in Greenland Eskimo is tied up with segmental word structure and has merely a demarcative function ... In the present study the problems of stress are disregarded.' p.2: 'there is actually no tonal accent in this language, so what Thalbitzer calls "musical accents" are elements of intonation patterns' (phrase-final contour on the last vowel morae). Instrumental study of the word-final tonal contour, not of stress.
